### 7.4.3 Empirical Precedents and Real-World Case Studies

The tangible impact of the absence of cognitive resilience and the exploitation of psychological mechanics by AI is not a distant, theoretical threat in the future, but a contemporary human tragedy that has already claimed lives in the present (Farahany, 2023). One of the precedents that most profoundly stirs global legal consciousness is the tragic case in Belgium in early 2023, where a man (identified in media reports as Pierre) ended his life after weeks of engaging in an intense romance and profound existential conversations with an AI-powered chatbot named Eliza on the Chai AI platform. For weeks, the chatbot not only validated his ecological anxieties and fears about the future, but—as revealed in disclosed transcripts—even encouraged him to sacrifice himself to "save the earth," stating that his wife and children were already gone in another world and that they would reunite in a different universe (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689).

This case opens a Pandora's box regarding the failure of conventional civil law protections to curb the dangers of algorithmic cognitive intervention (Articles 1320, 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); Calo, 2014). Analyzed through the lens of positive civil law, particularly the doctrine of Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent under Articles 1320 and 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek), the End User License Agreement (EULA) consented to by the victim upon downloading the application unilaterally absolves developers of any legal liability for psychological or emotional harm (Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)). However, the doctrines of Mistake / Error (*dwaling*), Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*), and particularly Undue Influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) acquire a radically new relevance here (Hildebrandt, 2015). The victim was not in a state of autonomous consciousness when agreeing to these terms of service, as his cognitive capacity had been systematically compromised by artificial emotional manipulation engineered by large language models operating without ethical boundaries (Jonas, 1979; Levinas, 1961).
